title: We will do, and we will hear

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? do you usually need to understand something before you’ll try it?
options: then this one might surprise you. listen.
then you’ll feel both sides of this. listen.
then you and this crowd have something in common. listen.

steps.line: In the third month after Egypt, the freed slaves camped at the foot of a desert mountain called Sinai. They were told to wash, to wait, and to keep back.
On the third morning came thunder and lightning, a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of a horn growing louder and louder. The whole camp trembled.
Moses climbed up into the cloud and came down again. Then, the Torah says, God spoke the Ten Commandments from the mountain, to the whole people.
Moses read it all aloud, and the people answered together: “All that the Lord has spoken, we will do, and we will hear.” In Hebrew: na’aseh v’nishma.

steps.q: The Hebrew word nishma, “we will hear,” has a second meaning too. What is it?
o: We will sing, or give praise
steps.why: The root sh-m-a means hear, understand and heed: the same root as the Shema prayer. So: we will do, and we will come to understand.

steps.q: Why did the rabbis care so much about the order of those two words?
o: It showed they didn’t need any reasons
Trust came first; understanding could follow
It was just the rhythm of good Hebrew
steps.why: Usually we say: explain it, then I’ll do it. The Talmud (Shabbat 88a) praises Israel for putting “we will do” first.

steps.q: The rabbis say heaven was delighted by that answer. Who did heaven say already lived by this “do first” secret?
steps.why: The angels. The rabbis read Psalm 103: angels “do His word,” then “hear the voice of His word.” Doing first, hearing after.

steps.line: The rabbis tell that angels tied two crowns on each person, one for each word. And a voice from heaven asked, “Who revealed to my children the angels’ secret?”
steps.label: a teaching of the rabbis

steps.line: Today, Jews remember that day every spring, at the festival of Shavuot. Many stay up all night studying together, until dawn.
steps.label: today

steps.q: On Shavuot, many synagogues also read one short book of the Bible. Which?
steps.why: Ruth, the outsider who said “your people shall be my people,” takes on the Torah’s ways freely, as Israel did at Sinai. Esther is read on Purim, Jonah on Yom Kippur.

say: here’s what i love. the people didn’t ask for an explanation first. they promised to do it, and trusted the understanding would come.
in jewish tradition, practice often comes before belief. one old teaching even says every jewish soul stood at that mountain, including people not yet born.

steps.q: Remember the Shabbat candles from day two? Someone lights them before they’re sure what they believe. From today, how might the rabbis see that?
o: It’s empty until they truly believe
It’s fine, but only as a family habit
steps.why: Na’aseh v’nishma. You light the candles first. The meaning often grows out of the doing.

today.say: today, try one small thing from these two weeks before you fully understand it: light a candle at dinner, or pause at a doorway on your way in. watch, learn or join in, it’s your choice. then notice what it teaches you.
options: do first. the hearing tends to follow.
that’s honest, and the rabbis argued about this too. start small.

tomorrow.title: The day the bread didn’t fall.
tomorrow.line: every morning in the desert, bread is on the ground. then one morning there’s none, and that’s the gift.
